title: Cicero sets him on fire (3.4)
hookLine: a book of philosophy makes him long for wisdom itself
tomorrow: what did his mother see in her dream?

cards: Required reading. The book you skim for the test and forget by summer. Augustine had one of those.
He was training to be a public speaker, and his course set a book by Cicero, the Roman orator, to study for its style. He read it for the sentences. Then the book did something nobody assigned.

teach.b: The book was the Hortensius, urging its reader toward philosophy, and Augustine explains the word: the love of wisdom is what the Greeks call philosophy.

The book turned his prayers toward God, he says, and made every empty hope look cheap. He longed, with a burning heart, for a wisdom that doesn't die. What delighted him was that Cicero pushed no single school.
Love wisdom itself, wherever it is.
One thing cooled him: the name of Christ wasn't in it, a name he'd drunk in, he says, with his mother's milk. So what is the love of wisdom for? Augustine's answer is that it's reaching for a person.

Paul names him, in the Douay-Rheims: "Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God." A neighbor says something close. In the Mishnah, in the sayings called Pirkei Avot, the sage Ben Zoma asks, who is wise?

teach.h: BEN ZOMA: LEARN FROM EVERY PERSON.
teach.b: And answers: the one who learns from every person. Augustine caught fire from a pagan's book; Ben Zoma would recognize that kind of learner. And one honest difference.
Avot's sayings sit among teachings on studying Torah, and the wisdom it prizes is learned there. For Augustine, the wisdom he longed for turned out to have a name, Christ.
Two traditions, each in its own words, both ready to learn from anyone.

how: Catholic seminarians study philosophy as part of their preparation for theology, and Catholic spiritual reading includes books meant to stir a longing for God.

games.q: what does “cicero sets him on fire” mean?
o: a burning ambition to win a public office
a well-known orator teaches him to speak well
a Roman book lights a longing for wisdom itself

games.q: the book that lit him — tap the pairs.
p: the wise learn from every person

s: reading Cicero made Augustine a Christian on the spot
it set him longing for wisdom; one name was missing from it, and the road was still long.
Cicero told him to love wisdom itself, not one school
that's what delighted him: seek wisdom wherever it is.
only Christians teach learning wisdom from outsiders
in Pirkei Avot, Ben Zoma says the wise person learns from every person.

games.q: a friend found real wisdom in a Roman philosopher's book and feels guilty, since it isn't Christian. what does Augustine's story offer her?
o: a good book can light the longing; then ask what it's for.
put it down; only Christian books are safe to learn from.
it doesn't matter what the longing reaches for, if it feels good.
games.why: Augustine thanks God for the fire Cicero lit, and names what was missing. he keeps both.

practice: Find one book on your shelf or your phone that once made you long for something wiser or truer, and look at its cover, or one line from it.
Rest your eyes there for a few breaths, then ask, without rushing an answer, what that longing is reaching for.

wordCard.voice: Cicero sets him on fire. A Roman book of philosophy turns Augustine from style toward the love of wisdom itself, though one name was missing from it.

orig.note: Latin for wisdom, what the Hortensius set Augustine longing for.

carryVoice: Your line: longing for wisdom, lit by a book and aimed at someone. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.q: Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God
